newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War adds to decline of Eastern Zaire's coffee crop.
newsitem.headline: War adds to decline of Eastern Zaire's coffee crop.

text.p: Growing fighting and suffering in Eastern Zaire are only the latest blow to a coffee region declining through poor infrastructure, labour shortage and disease, traders say.
The north-eastern region of Haut-Zaire (Upper Zaire) still accounts for around 20 percent of roughly 60,000 tonnes of annual robusta exports.

Worst affected by the fighting and influx of more than one million Hutu refugees is the around 5,500 tonne crop of high quality arabica coffee, grown exclusively along the hilly frontier with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
"This is only the latest blow and in terms of decline in the robusta crop other factors are certainly more significant at the moment," said one coffee trader in the regional capital, Kisangani.

Zaire has been fighting Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels who launched an offensive a month ago along the eastern border, spreading instability across a much larger region as both displaced Zaireans and Rwandan refugees fled.
Upper Zaire, until the late 1980s producing over 30 percent of the country's crop, has been hard hit by the collapse of the national transport system through decades of mismanagement and corruption.

"It is getting more and more expensive to transport coffee. The roads are so bad that the cost of bringing it from Isiro to Kisangani and then to Kinshasa means it is barely worth it unless world prices really climb," said one dealer.
Almost all Upper Zaire's robusta crop is shipped through the Atlantic port of Matadi more than 1,600 km (1,000 miles) away by road and river.

Upper Zaire has also been partcularly hard hit by the spread of the coffee fungus tracheomycose, as cash-strapped authorities have been unable to carry out any programme of destroying affected farms and compensating farmers.

"For the past few years we have been hit by a labour shortage as all the young men have rushed off to try digging diamonds in Kisangani," said the foreign owner of one plantation near Isiro, where crops have steadily declined.
"There is no way the plantation can be effective if it is not taken care of properly, and we simply cannot afford to hire workers enough to keep them and remain profitable."

Zaire's other coffee regions have not been as badly hit as Upper Zaire. Over the last coffee season for which figures are available national, exports increased to 65,005 tonnes from October 1994 to September 1995 against 59,756 tonnes a year earlier.

Dealers thank relative macroeconomic stability during the period as well as higher world prices in 1994, which encouraged many more people into the trade that is almost completely liberalised in Zaire.
Coffee has become an increasingly important source of foreign exchange for Zaire since political instability in the early 1990s literally decimated copper production.
Zaire's robusta exports go predominantly to Italy and Belgium for instant coffee roasting, where coffee tends to be drunk sweet and strength is a more important factor than quality.
